title: Regular GPS updates enable linkage of the child's movements over time
description: By transmitting live GPS coordinates at regular intervals, the child/source enables records from multiple moments to be linked into a continuous movement history for the same child, even if individual samples might seem innocuous in isolation.
assumptions: The backend or associated identifiers allow successive location samples to be associated with the same child/device/account.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include threat-tree node details.

title: Live GPS coordinates identify the child's whereabouts
description: The source shares precise, real-time location data that can directly or indirectly identify the child by revealing home, school, routines, and current whereabouts.
assumptions: Location precision and update frequency are sufficient to infer identity or uniquely single out the child.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is approximate; retrieved context only confirmed applicability of the threat type to this interaction.

title: In-transit location stream and metadata can be linked into a persistent trajectory
description: The data flow itself carries repeated GPS samples plus communication metadata such as timing, network identifiers, or session identifiers. These can be linked together to reconstruct a persistent trajectory for the same child/device.
assumptions: An observer on the flow or an intermediary can access payload and/or metadata sufficient to correlate transmissions.
uncertainty_note: Applies especially if transport metadata or payload are observable; exact tree node id is approximate.

title: Interception of live GPS data in transit reveals the child's location
description: If the flow is insufficiently protected, an eavesdropper could learn the child's current and historical locations from the transmitted coordinates or associated metadata.
assumptions: Transport protections may be absent, weak, misconfigured, or bypassed at some point in the communication path.
uncertainty_note: This is a genuine flow-level identifiability/disclosure risk, but likelihood depends strongly on actual transport security controls.

title: Backend can link successive GPS updates into a detailed movement profile
description: Upon receipt, the backend can correlate repeated location updates for the same child/account/device and build a longitudinal movement profile, linking visits, routines, and co-locations across time.
assumptions: The backend stores or processes identifiers that associate updates with the same child over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate due to missing threat-tree excerpt.

title: Backend processing of precise location data makes the child identifiable
description: The backend receives precise GPS coordinates that can identify or single out the child by inferring sensitive places such as home, school, and habitual routes.
assumptions: Backend has access to sufficiently precise coordinates and contextual data to infer identity or uniquely distinguish the child.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is approximate.

title: Backend learns sensitive personal information from location traces
description: The backend can derive private facts from the child's location history, such as daily routines, religious attendance, medical visits, school attendance, social relationships, or other sensitive behaviors.
assumptions: Location history is retained or analyzed with enough granularity to infer sensitive attributes or activities.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is based on best judgement; retrieved context did not provide disclosure subnodes.

title: Continuous location collection may be unexpected or insufficiently transparent to the child
description: If the backend collects live GPS coordinates at regular intervals without clear, age-appropriate explanation, the child may not understand the extent, frequency, or implications of the monitoring and downstream use.
assumptions: Transparency notices, UX cues, or child-appropriate explanations may be absent or inadequate.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on the surrounding notice/UX design, which is not fully described here; tree node id is approximate.

title: Backend collection of continuous child location data may exceed necessity or valid consent basis
description: Receiving live GPS coordinates at regular intervals for a child creates a risk that the processing is not compliant with data minimization, purpose limitation, retention limits, or child-specific consent/authorization requirements if such collection is broader than necessary for the stated purpose.
assumptions: Applicable legal or policy obligations require necessity, proportionality, and valid authorization for child location tracking.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends on jurisdiction, purpose, and governance controls; tree node id is approximate.

title: Backend stores precise location pings beyond what is necessary
description: The backend writes each location ping to persistent storage. If full-resolution, high-frequency location data is stored by default, this may disclose more personal data than is necessary for the service purpose, violating data minimization.
assumptions: Assumes the service could operate with less granular, less frequent, or shorter-retained location data than every raw ping.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimization concepts; exact subnode may differ in the canonical tree.

title: Stored location history enables linking of multiple records to the same individual
description: The Location History Store accumulates repeated location pings over time. This allows records from different times and contexts to be linked into a longitudinal movement profile for the same user or device.
assumptions: Assumes records contain a stable account, device, session, or other correlator enabling association over time.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro subnode id is approximate; applicability of linking itself is strong.

title: Persistent location history can identify a user through mobility patterns
description: A stored history of location pings can make a person identifiable, even if direct identifiers are absent, because home/work locations and unique movement patterns can single out an individual.
assumptions: Assumes the stored data includes sufficiently precise timestamps/coordinates or can be combined with other available data.
uncertainty_note: Subnode id is approximate; the identification risk from precise location history is well established.

title: Location history reveals sensitive habits and activities
description: By receiving and storing each location ping, the data store enables inference of visits, routines, associations, and sensitive places such as home, workplace, clinics, places of worship, or political events.
assumptions: Assumes the stored history is retained and queryable such that patterns and sensitive place visits can be inferred.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode id is best-effort; detectability/inference from location traces clearly applies.

title: Comprehensive location-history storage may exceed users' expectations
description: Users may not expect that every location ping is persistently stored as a historical record. If the backend writes all pings without clear notice or meaningful controls, the processing can be insufficiently transparent and therefore unaware to data subjects.
assumptions: Assumes notices/UX do not clearly explain continuous storage of raw location history or do not provide meaningful controls.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; threat depends on actual notice and consent/choice design.

title: Retention of raw location history may be incompatible with purpose limitation
description: Storing every location ping in the Location History Store may be unnecessary or incompatible with the original service purpose if retention periods, secondary uses, or granularity are not constrained. This creates a policy and compliance risk around lawful basis, minimization, and retention limitation.
assumptions: Assumes no strict retention schedule, purpose limitation, or aggregation strategy is enforced for the stored pings.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode id is approximate; non-compliance depends on the system's stated purposes, lawful basis, and retention policy.

title: Backend shares more precise location data than necessary for geofence evaluation
description: The backend forwards new location pings to the geofencing engine. If full-precision coordinates, persistent user identifiers, or unnecessary contextual attributes are sent when coarser location, pseudonymous identifiers, or reduced metadata would suffice, the act of sharing causes avoidable disclosure of personal data.
assumptions: Geofence checks may not require maximum coordinate precision or directly identifying account attributes on every ping.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement for unnecessary/overly detailed disclosure; exact sub-node naming may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Location pings in transit can directly identify a user or device
description: The flow carries fresh location pings from the backend to the geofencing engine. If the payload or transport metadata includes stable account, device, session, or API identifiers, the data in transit may directly identify the individual associated with the movement data.
assumptions: The flow contains or is correlated with stable identifiers rather than fully ephemeral tokens.
uncertainty_note: Exact identification sub-node may differ across threat-tree editions; applicability depends on whether stable identifiers are present on this flow.

title: Repeated location pings enable linkage of movements into a trackable trajectory
description: Even if each ping is not overtly identifying on its own, repeated transmissions over this flow can be linked by persistent identifiers, timing, routing metadata, or consistent payload structure to reconstruct a user's travel pattern and correlate events across time.
assumptions: Multiple pings from the same user/device are transmitted over time and can be associated with one another.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is selected by best judgement for linkability via repeated observations/metadata; exact numbering may vary.

title: Geofencing engine derives and retains sensitive presence information beyond the immediate alerting purpose
description: On receipt of location pings, the geofencing engine can infer zone entry/exit, presence at sensitive places, routines, and dwell times. If it stores or further uses these derived facts beyond what is strictly needed to determine current geofence events, it creates avoidable disclosure of additional personal data.
assumptions: The engine may persist derived geofence events, histories, or analytics rather than performing only transient evaluation.
uncertainty_note: Sub-node chosen by best judgement for disclosure through derivation/secondary processing; exact id may differ by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Geofencing evaluation may process location data for a purpose users would not reasonably expect
description: Users may expect location pings to support immediate zone entry/exit checks, but the receiving engine could also use them for profiling routines, hotspot analysis, or operational analytics. Such secondary use would make the processing purpose insufficiently transparent or unexpected from the user's perspective.
assumptions: The destination process has capabilities or incentives to reuse incoming location data beyond real-time geofence determination.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on actual downstream use at P2; if P2 performs only narrowly scoped real-time checks, this threat may not apply.

title: Location pings may be processed for geofencing without valid or sufficiently specific consent/legal basis
description: The destination process receives continuous location data to determine zone entry/exit. If users have not specifically agreed to this geofencing purpose, or if consent cannot be demonstrated or withdrawn effectively for this processing step, the receipt and use of the data may be non-compliant.
assumptions: Geofencing is optional or requires a distinct legal basis separate from basic app operation.
uncertainty_note: This is a genuine risk for location-based features, but applicability depends on the system's actual legal basis and consent design.

title: Configured zones disclose sensitive household routines and places
description: The Family Account & Permissions Store shares zone definitions such as home, school, and friends' houses with the Geofencing & Alert Engine. These locations reveal highly sensitive information about children and family routines, social relationships, and habitual whereabouts. The disclosure risk arises at the source because the store releases this sensitive configuration data for processing.
assumptions: Zone definitions are tied to a specific family or child account rather than being generic templates.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only provided applicable threat types/positions, not detailed node ids.

title: Zone-definition payload can identify a specific family or child
description: Data in transit contains named or semantically distinctive places such as home, school, and a friend's house. Even without explicit identifiers, this combination can identify or single out a particular family or child when correlated with external knowledge about addresses and schools.
assumptions: Zone definitions include coordinates, labels, or other semantics sufficient to distinguish households or children.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro node id may differ; identification via distinctive location sets is the intended threat.

title: Zone definitions enable linkage of multiple events and accounts
description: The set of configured geofences can act as a stable quasi-identifier. Repeated transmission or observation of the same home-school-other-location pattern may allow linking this flow to the same family across sessions, services, or datasets, even if direct identifiers are absent.
assumptions: The same or similar zone sets are reused over time and observable in transit or logs.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; linkage through stable location patterns is the core concern.

title: Geofencing engine learns more location context than strictly necessary
description: On receipt, the Geofencing & Alert Engine gains access to detailed configured places for the family. If the engine stores, analyzes, or exposes these definitions beyond what is necessary for boundary checks, it creates an unnecessary disclosure of intimate household and child-location context at the destination.
assumptions: P2 may persist, log, or otherwise process the zone definitions beyond transient in-memory use.
uncertainty_note: Applies if P2 retains or uses the received zone data beyond minimal geofence evaluation.

title: Secondary use of family place definitions for profiling or analytics
description: The destination process receives zone definitions for geofencing, but could repurpose them for analytics, behavioral profiling, feature improvement, or other purposes not expected by the family. Such use would exceed the original purpose of configuring alerts and constitutes an unawareness/unexpected-use privacy threat.
assumptions: Families reasonably expect these locations to be used only to evaluate geofence events and alerts.
uncertainty_note: Classified under Unawareness based on potential unexpected secondary use; some methodologies might also discuss this under policy/compliance concerns.

title: Processing of children's sensitive location settings may lack valid consent or legal basis
description: The Geofencing & Alert Engine processes configured locations that can concern children and reveal home, school, and social contacts. If this processing occurs without appropriately informed parental authorization, age-appropriate transparency, or another valid legal basis, the destination's receipt and use of the data may be non-compliant.
assumptions: The service is subject to privacy regulation and the configured zones relate to identifiable children or family members.
uncertainty_note: Specific compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and product context; node id is approximate.

title: Notification content discloses the child's location event to the parent
description: By sending an arrival/departure alert, the geofencing engine discloses personal information about the child's whereabouts and movement events. This is an inherent privacy threat on this flow if the disclosure is broader, more frequent, or more detailed than necessary for the intended purpose.
assumptions: The alert contains at least the fact that a specific child entered or exited a defined zone, and that this is personal data.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only confirms applicable threat types/positions, not detailed node ids.

title: Repeated geofence alerts enable linkability of the child's movement patterns
description: Even if each alert is individually simple, a sequence of arrival/departure notifications on this flow can be linked over time to build a movement profile for the same child and household, revealing routines such as school, home, or extracurricular attendance.
assumptions: The parent can associate repeated alerts with the same child or account over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the threat clearly concerns linkability across multiple events on this flow.

title: Alert metadata can identify the child or household
description: Identifiers or quasi-identifiers in the notification payload or transport metadata—such as child name, account identifier, device token, zone label, timestamps, or endpoint addressing—may allow identification of the child or parent household.
assumptions: The notification or its surrounding metadata contains stable identifiers or distinctive combinations of attributes.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the identification risk is grounded in payload and transport metadata rather than only explicit names.

title: Parent-side retention or onward sharing of alerts causes further disclosure
description: Once received, the parent may store, screenshot, forward, or otherwise share the arrival/departure alerts, causing additional disclosure of the child's location history beyond the original intended context.
assumptions: The destination external entity is capable of retaining or redisclosing the notifications.
uncertainty_note: This is a genuine destination-side disclosure risk, but exact downstream handling by the parent is not specified.

title: The child may be unaware that geofence transitions trigger parent notifications
description: If the system does not adequately inform the child or relevant data subject that entering or leaving a zone automatically generates alerts to the parent, the processing lacks sufficient transparency and predictability.
assumptions: The child is a data subject whose awareness matters in the system context, and transparency mechanisms may be limited or absent.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on the product's notice model and the role of the child as a data subject.

title: Automatic geofence alerts may exceed the data subject's consent or choice expectations
description: Pushing notifications for every zone entry/exit may conflict with the child's or account holder's consent choices if alerts are enabled by default, are too granular, or continue after preferences should have limited such sharing.
assumptions: Consent, parental controls, or privacy preferences are relevant to whether these notifications should be sent.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on the system's consent/preference design, which is not described in the prompt.

title: Parent discloses excessive child data during registration
description: The parent provides highly sensitive child profile data (name, date of birth, school) and geofence definitions when creating the account. If all fields are collected by default without clear necessity for initial registration, the act of sharing may disclose more personal data about the child than is needed at this stage.
assumptions: Assumes some of the submitted child attributes or geofence details are optional or not strictly necessary for account creation.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on general disclosure-by-oversharing at the source; exact sub-node may vary in the project taxonomy.

title: Child and parent can be identified from registration data in transit
description: The transmitted payload contains direct identifiers and quasi-identifiers, including the child's name, date of birth, school, and the parent's account details. Interception or observation of the flow could enable identification of the child and parent.
assumptions: Assumes the flow may be observable to network intermediaries or logs if transport protections or minimization are insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree sub-node may differ depending on whether identification is modeled via content or metadata.

title: Registration payload enables linkage of child records across contexts
description: Combining child name, date of birth, school, and geofence-related location context can allow this child profile to be linked with records from other services or datasets, especially where school and birth date are shared attributes.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker or recipient has access to auxiliary datasets or repeated observations of similar payloads.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort node selection for linkability from data content in transit.

title: Geofence definitions disclose sensitive location patterns in transit
description: Geofence zones reveal places significant to the child and family, such as home, school, or routine destinations. Exposure of these zones during transmission discloses sensitive location information and daily-life patterns.
assumptions: Assumes geofence data includes precise coordinates, addresses, or semantically meaningful place labels.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node may vary depending on whether location privacy is represented under disclosure of content or inference from content.

title: Backend may store and process more child data than necessary
description: Upon receipt, the backend may retain full child identity data and precise geofence zones even if only part of that information is needed for service provisioning. This creates a disclosure risk through unnecessary storage and internal processing of sensitive child and location data.
assumptions: Assumes the backend stores raw submitted fields rather than minimizing, truncating, or separating them by purpose.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort for disclosure due to unnecessary collection/retention at the destination.

title: Backend can link parent identity, child identity, school, and geofence data
description: The backend receives all submitted attributes in one transaction and can associate the parent account with the child's identity, school, and significant locations. This enables strong linkage across family, educational, and location contexts.
assumptions: Assumes the backend stores these attributes under a common account or profile identifier.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort node selection for destination-side linkability.

title: Backend can uniquely identify the child from combined profile attributes
description: Even if some fields are not unique alone, the combination of child name, date of birth, school, and associated parent account is likely sufficient to uniquely identify the child within the service and potentially beyond it.
assumptions: Assumes ordinary backend access to all submitted fields and no immediate pseudonymization on receipt.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node may differ depending on local threat-tree granularity.

title: Backend use of child profile and geofence data may be insufficiently transparent
description: After receiving the registration and profile data, the backend may process or retain the child's identity, school, and geofence information for purposes not obvious to the parent, such as analytics, profiling, or long-term retention, reducing user unawareness about how the data is used.
assumptions: Assumes privacy notices or in-context explanations are incomplete or not specific about downstream uses.
uncertainty_note: Included because the flow description does not indicate transparency controls; applicability depends on actual notice and consent design.

title: Backend may process child and location data without valid consent or appropriate parental authorization controls
description: The backend receives personal data about a child and sensitive location-related geofence information. If the service does not verify that the submitting adult is authorized to create the child's profile or does not capture and honor valid permissions for this processing, the collection may be non-compliant.
assumptions: Assumes the system has legal or policy obligations to verify parental authority and establish a valid basis for processing child and location data.
uncertainty_note: Exact node may vary by whether the taxonomy distinguishes consent, legal basis, and children's data obligations.

title: Backend stores more child/account/geofence data than necessary
description: The backend sends account details, child profile attributes, and geofence zone data to the permissions store. If fields beyond what is strictly required for authorization and family-account management are persisted, this creates avoidable disclosure through over-collection and over-storage of personal data, especially sensitive child-related and location-related information.
assumptions: DS2 is used for family account and permission management; not every child-profile or geofence attribute may be necessary for that purpose.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is based on best-fit minimality/explicit disclosure reasoning from LINDDUN Pro; exact subnode label may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Stored family, child, and geofence records can be linked into a consolidated profile
description: By receiving and storing account data together with child profile and geofence zone data, the data store can enable linkage of identity, family relationships, and location semantics across records. This may allow creation of a richer profile of a child and household than users expect.
assumptions: DS2 stores these data under common account or family identifiers and supports retrieval across them.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro subnode may differ depending on whether linkage is modeled as record linkage or cross-context correlation; this is a best-fit node choice.

title: Child or parent identities may be directly identifiable in the permissions store
description: If the stored account and child profile data include direct identifiers such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, account IDs, or stable child identifiers, the destination store holds data that can identify specific individuals, including minors.
assumptions: The payload likely contains direct or persistent identifiers needed for account management.
uncertainty_note: Subnode chosen as a generic direct-identifiability case; exact numbering may vary across LINDDUN Pro materials.

title: Geofence and profile data enable inference of sensitive habits or home/school locations
description: Once stored together, geofence zones and child profile/account context may allow inference of sensitive information such as home address, school, daily routines, custody patterns, or other behavioral traits, even if those facts were not explicitly provided in the flow.
assumptions: Geofence zones are meaningful places or coordinates associated with a child or family account.
uncertainty_note: This is a strong inference risk, but exact sensitivity depends on the granularity of geofence data and associated metadata.

title: Secondary use of stored child and geofence data may exceed user expectations
description: Data stored in the family account and permissions store could later be used for analytics, feature development, behavioral monitoring, or other purposes beyond the immediate need to manage permissions and family accounts. Such downstream use may be unexpected, particularly for child-related and location-related data.
assumptions: Purpose limitation controls are not guaranteed merely because the data are stored in DS2.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on governance and purpose-limitation controls not visible from the flow alone.

title: Storage of child profile and geofence data may be incompatible with consent or parental expectation
description: Persisting child profile and geofence zone data in the permissions store may go beyond the scope of consent or reasonable parental expectation if users were not clearly informed that these categories would be stored here for this purpose. This is especially relevant for minors' data and location-related information.
assumptions: Consent, notice, or another legal basis may be limited to core app functionality and may not explicitly cover all stored attributes in DS2.
uncertainty_note: Compliance assessment depends on actual notices, consent flows, contracts, and jurisdictional requirements, which are not provided.

title: Parent request reveals interest in the child's whereabouts
description: By initiating a request to view the child's current location or location history, the parent discloses to the backend that they are seeking information about a specific child at a specific time. This can expose sensitive intent or circumstances, such as monitoring routines or concern about the child's movements.
assumptions: The backend can associate the request with a specific parent account and child profile.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only provided applicability by threat type/position, not detailed threat-tree nodes.

title: Request metadata can link parent and child identities in transit
description: Even if the payload is protected, metadata on the flow such as account identifiers, child identifiers, session tokens, timing, and repeated request patterns can enable linking a particular parent to a particular child and to recurring monitoring behavior.
assumptions: Observable metadata exists on the communication path or in intermediary network/service logs.
uncertainty_note: Threat applies primarily to transport metadata and intermediary observability; exact exposure depends on deployment and transport protections.

title: Flow metadata may identify the parent or child
description: Identifiers or quasi-identifiers carried on the request flow, such as account IDs, device identifiers, child IDs, IP address, or stable session information, may allow an observer or intermediary to identify the requesting parent and the child whose location is being queried.
assumptions: The flow or its surrounding metadata contains stable identifiers or can be correlated with other data.
uncertainty_note: Best-judgement tree-node id; exact identifiability depends on protocol design and logging practices.

title: Request contents disclose sensitive location-related interests in transit
description: The request itself may disclose that the parent is asking for current location or historical location data, which reveals sensitive information about the child and the parent's monitoring activity if exposed on the network path or to intermediaries.
assumptions: Request payload or metadata is visible to some intermediary, endpoint security product, or logging component.
uncertainty_note: If strong end-to-end transport protection and minimal logging are in place, likelihood is reduced.

title: Backend can link repeated location-view requests to a parent-child relationship
description: On receipt, the backend can correlate repeated requests over time and link a specific parent account to a specific child, building a detailed picture of the relationship and monitoring frequency.
assumptions: The backend stores account, child, and request records with persistent identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id chosen by best judgement due to lack of detailed node mapping in retrieved context.

title: Backend learns sensitive behavioral patterns from location-view requests
description: Processing and storing requests to view current or historical location can reveal sensitive behavioral information, such as when parents check on children, which children are monitored more closely, and possible inferences about school, home, medical visits, or emergencies.
assumptions: The backend logs requests or retains analytics/telemetry about map and history access.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on retention and analytics practices at the destination.

title: Backend may process the request for secondary purposes beyond the parent's expectation
description: The backend may use request data for analytics, profiling, service optimization, employee access, or other secondary purposes that are not transparent to the parent, making the processing of this location-related request insufficiently understandable or predictable.
assumptions: The service performs internal logging, analytics, or secondary processing not fully explained at request time.
uncertainty_note: Included as an unawareness threat only insofar as the destination's processing may be opaque; exact applicability depends on notices and consent UX.

title: Backend retention or reuse of location-view requests may exceed consent or policy
description: If the backend stores or reuses the parent's request to access current or historical child location beyond what was consented to or beyond stated policy, the processing may be non-compliant with consent, purpose limitation, or data minimization requirements.
assumptions: The system retains request logs or analytics tied to identifiable users and children.
uncertainty_note: Compliance impact depends on the actual legal basis, parental authority model, and published retention/processing policy.

title: Excessive disclosure of detailed location history from the store
description: The location history store may provide more historical location data than is necessary for the parent's requested map/history view, such as overly long retention windows, overly fine-grained coordinates, or records for broader time ranges than requested. The act of sharing this rich history from the store creates a disclosure risk because location traces are highly sensitive and reveal routines and habits.
assumptions: Assumes the backend query can retrieve broader or more granular history than is strictly needed for the requested feature.

title: Linkability via repeated retrievals of the same child's location history
description: Repeated transfers of stored location history over this flow can enable linking multiple requests and sessions to the same child or family account, especially through stable identifiers, query parameters, or consistent record structure. Even if payload access is controlled, metadata on the flow can support correlation of the same data subject across events.
assumptions: Assumes requests or responses on this flow carry stable identifiers or otherwise correlatable metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the retrieved context confirms L applies to DataStore->Process flows but does not provide the detailed node list.

title: Identifiability from location-history payload or transfer metadata
description: The transferred location history may directly identify a child or household through account identifiers, device identifiers, home/school coordinates, or distinctive movement patterns. Even if explicit names are absent, the combination of trajectory data and transfer metadata can make the data subject identifiable.
assumptions: Assumes the stored history includes precise timestamps/coordinates or identifiers typical for serving a map/history feature.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate due to missing detailed threat-tree context.

title: Backend processes retrieved location history beyond what is necessary for the view
description: On receipt, the backend may retain, cache, enrich, or reuse the child's location history for purposes beyond rendering the parent's map/history view, such as analytics, debugging, or secondary profiling. This constitutes disclosure/use of sensitive location data at the destination beyond the immediate need.
assumptions: Assumes backend-side caching, logging, analytics, or reuse is possible after retrieval.
uncertainty_note: Threat categorized under Disclosure of information because the privacy harm arises from backend-side exposure or secondary use; exact tree-node id is approximate.

title: Use of location history for a purpose incompatible with the parent's requested view
description: The backend may use retrieved location history for purposes not expected by the data subject or not compatible with serving the parent's map/history view, such as behavioral analytics, model training, or operational monitoring. This creates a policy/purpose-limitation privacy threat at the destination.
assumptions: Assumes no strict technical or organizational controls prevent secondary use once the backend has retrieved the data.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; detailed U threat-tree nodes were not provided in the retrieved context.

title: Insufficient transparency or consent alignment for backend retrieval of location history
description: If users or guardians were not clearly informed that historical location traces would be retrieved and processed by the backend for this feature, or if this retrieval exceeds the scope of obtained consent or another legal basis, the destination processing may be non-compliant. The privacy issue arises when the backend receives and processes the data without adequate notice, choice, or governance alignment.
assumptions: Assumes consent/notice/legal-basis constraints apply to historical child-location processing in this system.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends strongly on the system's notices, consent model, and jurisdiction; exact tree-node id is approximate.

title: Parent may disclose the child's location-sharing relationship to an unintended or wrong secondary guardian
description: By initiating an invitation for a secondary guardian to view the child's location, the parent shares personal data about the child and the parent-child relationship. If the parent selects the wrong recipient, misunderstands the invite scope, or is socially pressured into inviting someone inappropriate, the act of sharing itself causes disclosure of sensitive relationship and location-access information.

description: The invitation flow may contain direct identifiers (e.g. email address, phone number, account identifier, child name) or indirect identifiers that allow identification of the parent, child, or invitee while the data is in transit.

title: Invitation metadata can link parent, child, and secondary guardian accounts
description: Even if content is minimized, metadata on this flow can reveal that a specific parent is attempting to connect a specific secondary guardian to a specific child account or household. This creates a new link between identities and roles that may be privacy-sensitive.
assumptions: Backend or intermediaries can observe sender, recipient, child/account context, or stable identifiers/tokens associated with the invitation.
